title: runners.toml implement cell still carries the deleted pi CLI's --approve
body:
The tick's named target: .tick/runners.toml [roles.implement] still declares args = ["--approve"] (line 22) under a comment that explains the deleted pi CLI's project-local file-trust flag as if it launched (lines 13-19). Nothing can read it: the roles table's args have exactly one consumer, spawnArgv in internal/cli/executor.go, reached only when a herdr dispatch compiles an agent's argv, and runconfig.Compile refuses kind "pi" for a herdr pane since uxi; since 2q5 implement routes onto the local-subprocess executor, which launches the durable pi host from its own runner table, and a cloud container is booted from the worker.json its sandbox door hands it. A sweep resolving implement through runconfig.LoadForConfig on every substrate, every named config and every tier finds 22 findings carrying this line on the untouched tree. The protected_change is the whole replacement content of the file, byte-verified against this tree: it drops the line, replaces the trust story with the reason there are no args, and corrects the one other stale claim in the same cell family (opus IS an implement rung locally, at frontier, and in the cloud's named claude config). Every value line is unchanged; with the comment lines removed the new file is the old one minus the dead line. Same cell and words as open tick 2p3.
evidence: .tick/runners.toml:13-22; internal/cli/executor.go:301 (spawnArgv, the only consumer); internal/runconfig/compile.go:159 (the pi/herdr refusal)
protected change: a new .tick/runners.toml (applied by the run after its close-out, for the merger to review)
protected_content:
# Worker routing for herd-substrate epic runs. Schema and semantics: the ticks
# skill's references/runners-config.md.
version = 2

[orchestration]
substrate = "auto"
max_parallel = 4

[roles.implement]
# Operator routing for Phase 2 (2026-09-10; the args line and the trust
# comment it carried are gone since tick q6z). Implementation runs on GLM on
# cloudflare through pi: GLM 5.3 for complex work (the default, and the
# `strong` tier) and GLM 5.3-flash for simple work (`economy`). opus is a
# claude-harness model, not a pi one: for implement it is the local frontier
# escalation and the cloud's named claude config only, never a starting tier
# — review and closeout are the roles the cells below run on it.
#
# No `args` on this cell, deliberately (tick q6z). The roles table's args
# have exactly one consumer — spawnArgv, in internal/cli/executor.go, read
# only when a herdr dispatch compiles an agent's argv — and
# runconfig.Compile refuses kind "pi" for a herdr pane (uxi), so no
# implement dispatch can read a flag from here: since 2q5 implement routes
# onto the local-subprocess executor, which launches the durable pi host
# from its own runner table (internal/exec/subprocess), and a cloud
# container is booted from the worker.json its sandbox door hands it. The
# line that sat here was the deleted pi CLI's `--approve` — project-local
# file trust, verified live 2026-09-10 (tick gjk;
# .tick/logs/herd/av8/gjk.RESULT.md) — dead config on every substrate since
# the CLI went with its worker path (jhp, uxi): it told a reader of this
# file that implement workers somewhere run with --approve. pi needs no
# permission-bypass flag in any case: it runs tools unprompted.
kind = "pi"
model = "cloudflare-workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3"
effort = "high"

# Simple work: mechanical, compiler-guided, low judgement.
[roles.implement.tiers.economy]
model = "cloudflare-workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash"
effort = "medium"

# Complex work, named explicitly. Same model as the default: GLM 5.3 IS the
# strong tier for this epic. opus is not a starting tier for implement
# anywhere: locally it is the frontier escalation only (runners.local.toml)
# and in the cloud only the named claude config's strong rung — and it is a
# claude-harness model, not a pi one.
[roles.implement.tiers.strong]
model = "cloudflare-workers-ai/@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3"
effort = "high"

# `balanced` is NOT declared for implement, deliberately (epic 43y, tick
# 7ml): until 2026-10-05 this cell named kind = "codex" (a Phase-2
# leftover), and because runners.local.toml declares no [roles.implement]
# role cell to overlay it away, a local run pinning --tier balanced
# dispatched an implement worker on the codex CLI — a worker harness that is
# neither pi-durable nor the claude-CLI frontier rung the operator's
# 2026-10-04 decision keeps. No ladder ever derives balanced (the local
# ladder climbs strong -> frontier, the cloud's economy -> strong), and in
# the cloud this cell never reached a container anyway (the cloud's own role
# cell applied last). With the cell gone, a pin of balanced is REFUSED
# naming the tier — the profile layer's fail-closed rule (a tier that
# silently falls back to the role is a tier an operator paid for and did not
# get) — and internal/reconcile's routing guard resolves every tier name
# a pin can reach on every substrate, so a cell like the old one cannot come
# back unnoticed.

# The frontier-tier review at epic completion — and, with [roles.closeout]
# below, the deliberate LOCAL claude exception the operator blessed
# (2026-10-04/05 decisions; tick j6o): local final reviews and close-outs
# run on the claude CLI on purpose — the hn6 run was moved to a local run
# for exactly that — so these cells name claude opus and
# runners.local.toml deliberately declares no review or closeout cell to
# overlay them away. The claude CLI is otherwise the local FRONTIER rung
# only: implementation runs on pi-durable at base and every tier but
# frontier, and the cloud overlays every cell here away
# (runners.cloud.toml applies last; nothing in the cloud runs claude).
# TestThisRepositorysLocalClaudeRoutingIsExactlyTheBlessedCells holds this
# table: claude exactly here and on implement's frontier rung, pi or a
# named refusal everywhere else, on every local substrate.
[roles.review]
kind = "claude"
model = "opus"
effort = "high"

# The ceiling-tier overlay of the review cell (tick 2p6): the resolve-conflict
# job — dispatched when two same-wave attempts meet a content or add/add
# conflict — routes at the policy's ceiling through the REVIEW cell's
# candidates (a dedicated [roles.resolve-conflict] cell would always win),
# and locally the ceiling is the frontier tier of .tick/runners.local.toml's
# ladder. Without this cell the overlay the ceiling asks for is refused, and
# a refused routing is a resolve that stops the run over config — which is
# why a run now refuses at START when it cannot route (reconcile.CheckRouting).
# The cloud merges this cell, but can never run it: runners.cloud.toml's
# review cell applies last and routes the job to a Workers AI model, and the
# cloud must declare its OWN ceiling's tier there (its ceiling is strong, not
# frontier). Nothing in the cloud runs claude.
[roles.review.tiers.frontier]
kind = "claude"
model = "opus"
effort = "high"

# Closeout shares the review cell's blessing (see [roles.review] above):
# the operator wants local close-outs on claude opus too — the same
# 2026-10-05 decision, recorded on tick j6o — and the cloud overlays this
# cell away exactly as it overlays review's. A local override that moves
# either cell off the claude CLI is a change to an operator decision, not
# a config edit: take it to the operator.
[roles.closeout]
kind = "claude"
model = "opus"
effort = "high"

# Findings a worker routes to ANOTHER repository (a `target` other than this
# one). This run cannot fix another repository, so such a finding never gates
# this epic; the run disposes of it with nobody triaging. A target listed here
# with `file = true` is filed by the run as a tick in that repository's own
# tracker, pushed to its default branch; any other target — or a filing that
# fails terminally — becomes a backlog tick HERE that names the target. The
# epic-2jn close-out held on five findings for pengelbrecht/ticks (2026-09-27)
# because neither path existed. The operator owns both repositories.
[findings.route."pengelbrecht/ticks"]
file = true

# The cloud's routing lives in .tick/runners.cloud.toml and a laptop's
# extras (the claude ladder) in .tick/runners.local.toml (tick 5uo): each
# merges over this file for its own world, and its role cells apply LAST, so
# nothing written here for a tier can reach a container.

[testing.commands]
# Spelled out, not `make gate`: this file is what says what the gate runs, and a
# reader must be able to see it here. The Makefile's `gate` target carries the
# same line for humans and CI, and a test fails if the two ever disagree — the
# gate had drifted to a bare `go test -short -count=1 ./...`, losing the timeout
# and the parallelism that keep internal/reconcile inside go's per-package
# limit, and nothing noticed.
#
# 2026-09-18 — the `-count=1` is dropped, deliberately, by the operator.
#
# It disabled Go's test cache, so every package was re-run for every tick even
# when nothing it depends on had changed. Epic 9pd ran this gate 49 times at
# roughly 20 minutes idle and 45-60+ under load, and finished with three ticks
# whose code was already merged facing three sequential full runs.
#
# The suite still runs in full. What changes is that a package whose inputs are
# unchanged answers from cache, which is a true statement about this tree: Go
# keys the cache on the package's sources, its dependencies, and the files and
# environment the test consulted.
#
# 2026-09-20 — and until tick 6wh it bought NOTHING, because the gate ran in a
# fresh temp directory every time and Go's cache keys on the absolute paths a
# test opened. The reasoning above was right and the mechanism was broken. 6wh
# runs the gate in a stable directory per repository, so the saving described
# here is now a thing that actually happens.
#
# The exposure that came with it, and the answer. A test that reads a file by an
# ABSOLUTE path OUTSIDE the module can be served from cache after that file
# changes. contracts.RepoRoot() builds absolute paths, so the drift guards that
# read this very file — TestThisRepositorysGateIsReadable,
# TestTheGateTargetMatchesTheDeclaredGate,
# TestTheHarnessBoundOutlivesEveryDeclaredGateBound — were the ones to watch.
# They are safe: this file is INSIDE the module those tests belong to, and go
# invalidates on it. Demonstrated by hand (edit the command on the line below
# and the guard fails, uncached) and on every run by
# TestACachedPassCannotHideAnEditToAFileAGuardReads, which rebuilds the guards'
# exact shape in a throwaway module and edits its input under it. `make suite`
# keeps -count=1 and remains the paranoid answer; it is no longer a required
# one. The wider audit is still tick mbv's.
#
# 2026-09-20 — the `-short` in this line now MEANS something (tick miu). It
# used to mean nothing: 6 of 215 test files consulted testing.Short(), so every
# per-tick gate ran the entire end-to-end suite — 23 minutes on the e9n
# attempt-8 run, which then failed on two tests (e4u, 7c0) that pass on a quiet
# host and stopped the Phase 5 run for nothing.
#
# internal/reconcile, internal/exec/herdr and internal/runstate now skip under
# -short at their harness constructors, and this command runs in seconds. What
# it no longer covers is exactly what CI covers: ci.yml's go job runs
# `make test-short` AND `make test`, so nothing this gate skips reaches main
# unrefused. internal/shorttest holds the guard that stops a new test from
# quietly re-entering — or quietly escaping — the short suite.
#
# The command itself is UNCHANGED, and must stay byte-identical to the
# Makefile's `gate` recipe: TestTheGateTargetMatchesTheDeclaredGate compares
# the two.
# gofmt and go vet first, exactly as CI's go job runs them: the gate is what a
# worker's commit must pass, and a gate weaker than CI lets a tick close on a
# tree CI then fails. An xte worker's unformatted test file did exactly that on
# 2026-09-23 - gate green, epic PR red - and the close-out held on it.
# `(! grep .)` prints any unformatted file and fails if there was one; it is
# written without $ so the Makefile's gate target can carry the same line.
go = { command = "gofmt -l . | grep -v '^contracts/' | (! grep .) && go vet ./... && go test -short -timeout 45m -parallel 12 ./...", description = "Go: gofmt, vet and tests, as CI runs them" }

# The TypeScript half, added by tick odc. Until it, NOTHING ran cloud/factory's
# tests — not this gate, not CI — and the cost of that silence was tick b9w: the
# control plane sat pinned to contract bundle 3.0.0 against a 5.2.0 bundle,
# wrong about three record shapes, for two major versions.
#
# What is here and what is NOT is a measurement, not a preference. On this host:
# pnpm install from a warm store 1s, contracts:check under 1s, tsc --noEmit 2s,
# vitest 82s. Gate commands run SERIALLY, so vitest would take the gate from
# 3m26s to about 4m48s on every tick — and the gate's speed is what made this
# epic survivable at all.
#
# So the gate takes the two cheap checks and CI takes vitest, where it runs as
# its own job beside the 7m15s Go job and costs no wall clock at all. The split
# is stated rather than implied: THIS GATE COVERS CONTRACTS AND TYPES, NOT
# BEHAVIOUR. A behavioural TypeScript regression is caught by CI on the epic PR,
# before anything reaches main, and never by this line.
#
# contracts:check is the one that earns its place here: it is the check that
# would have caught b9w's drift the day it happened, and it costs a second.
#
# `pnpm lint` is Biome (tick ncr) — this side's gofmt AND its vet, in one Rust
# binary. It is IN this command rather than a sibling [testing.commands] entry
# for one measured reason: a sibling would repeat `pnpm install`, which is ~0.7s
# on a warm store, to learn nothing the &&-chain's own output does not already
# name. Biome itself is 0.47/0.55/0.64s over three runs on these 109 files, so
# the gate's TypeScript half goes from ~3s to ~3.6s and the whole gate is
# unmoved against the 3m26s Go side.
#
# `pnpm lint` is `biome ci --error-on-warnings`, and the flag matters: plain
# `biome ci` exits 0 with warnings still on the floor, and most of what Biome
# found here — the unused variable, the implicit anys — is warning severity, so
# without it this half cannot refuse what it was added to catch.
#
# This is still CONTRACTS AND TYPES, not behaviour: Biome reads one file at a
# time and answers about its shape, not about what the Worker does.
#
# The two-layout fallback is GONE (tick 9a8). It existed only while Phase 4's
# l9n moved cloud/factory to cloudflare/: this command is read from the RUN'S
# checkout while it runs against the MERGED tree (defect 19q), so across the
# move the two disagreed and l9n could never have passed the gate whose job it
# was to move. Phase 4 merged to main on 2026-09-19 and neither cloud/factory
# nor cloud/sandbox exists any more, so the fallback arm named nothing.
ts = { command = "cd cloudflare && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline && pnpm lint && pnpm contracts:check && pnpm exec tsc --noEmit", description = "TypeScript format, lint, contracts and types" }

[environment.commands]
which-go = { command = "which go", description = "Go toolchain on PATH" }
git-config-user-email = { command = "git config user.email", description = "git identity configured" }
